## Keep test setup inline until repetition hides what differs between tests

_medium · any_

**Rule.** Write a test's data and setup inline first. Extract a helper once repetition hides what differs between
tests; it takes overrides and returns what the test needs, with no branch per case, so a reader sees the
difference between two similar tests at once.

**Why.** A shared helper with an `if` for every case makes the reader step through it to learn what one test does,
and copied setups bury the one line that differs.

## Derive the expected value from the test's own input, not a repeated literal

_medium · any_

**Rule.** When the expected value follows from the test's input, take it straight from that input: the row
count from the list the test rendered, a field's value from the value the test prefilled. When the
code under test computes the result, state it as a literal and do not repeat the formula.

**Why.** A hard-coded copy of the input goes stale the moment the input changes, so the test fails for a
reason unrelated to the code, or keeps passing against the wrong number. A repeated formula repeats
the bug it should catch.

## Name each test after the behaviour it checks, the situation and the expected outcome

_medium · any_

**Rule.** Name a test case after one behaviour: the situation and the outcome its caller sees
(`test_returning_an_overdue_book_charges_a_fine`, "rejects an empty title"). Never name it after the
method it calls or a number (`test_return_book`, `test_2`).

**Why.** A failure line that reads `test_return_book FAILED` does not say what broke, and a test named after
a method grows one more assertion for every behaviour the method gains.

## Add new tests to the project's existing suite, in the file for their topic

_medium · python, pytest_

**Rule.** Put a new test in the module's existing test directory under `tests/`, in the file that already holds its topic (status cases beside the other status cases, race tests beside the other race tests). Before you write, check which cases an existing test already proves and write only the rest; a case is never written twice. When two tests cover one case, keep the stronger one and move any assertion only the other had into it. A weak existing test is fixed in place, see `testing/principles/every-test-must-be-able-to-fail`; after merging suites, run the guard mutants again, because a guard may have been left with a single test.

**Why.** A status code changes in one suite while the copy of that case in a second suite still asserts the old value and stays green, so the same behaviour has to be updated, and can be forgotten, in two places (a second directory once repeated the status table and the race tests).

**Incorrect:**

```
tests/orders/
  test_api.py          # status cases
  test_concurrency.py  # race tests
tests_extra/orders/
  test_status.py       # the same status cases again
  test_races.py        # the same race tests again
```

**Correct:**

```
tests/orders/
  test_api.py          # status cases, the missing ones added here
  test_concurrency.py  # race tests, the weak one strengthened here
```

**Exceptions.** A suite that needs a run of its own (end-to-end against a deployed environment, load tests, a nightly fuzz run) is not a parallel suite and may live in its own directory, run from its own named target and a scheduled CI job. A directory that belongs to the normal check is registered as in `tooling/python/register-every-test-directory-in-the-check-gate`.

## Control the clock with time-machine, not hand-patched datetime

_medium · python, pytest, time-machine_

**Rule.** Freeze or move time with `@time_machine.travel(...)` instead of patching `datetime` yourself.

**Why.** A hand-written patch replaces `datetime` in one module only, so code that imported it elsewhere keeps reading the real clock and the test passes or fails by the hour.

**Incorrect:**

```python
with patch("myapp.billing.datetime"):
    make_invoice()   # reports.py imports datetime itself and still sees real time
```

**Correct:**

```python
@time_machine.travel("2026-11-05 12:00", tick=False)
def test_invoice_is_due_in_30_days():
    assert make_invoice().due == date(2026, 12, 5)
```

## Mirror the package in tests/ by domain module, never by test kind

_medium · python, pytest_

**Rule.** Give each domain module one directory under `tests/` with the module's name, and put all of its
tests there in topic files (`test_domain.py`, `test_service.py`, `test_api.py`). Mark a test's kind
with a registered marker such as `integration`, never with a `unit/`, `integration/` or `e2e/`
folder.

**Why.** Folders by kind spread one module's tests over three trees, so moving or deleting the module leaves
orphaned tests behind and a reader cannot see in one place what the module's tests cover.

**Incorrect:**

```text
tests/
├── unit/orders/test_service.py
├── integration/orders/test_repository.py
└── e2e/test_orders_api.py
```

**Correct:**

```text
tests/
└── orders/
    ├── test_service.py
    ├── test_repository.py   # SQL subclass marked integration
    └── test_api.py
```

**Exceptions.** A suite that needs a run of its own (a deployed environment, a schedule) gets its own top-level
directory, as `testing/python/guides/test-suite-layout` describes.

## Install pytest-randomly and pytest-timeout so hidden coupling and hangs fail loudly

_medium · python, pytest_

**Rule.** Add `pytest-randomly` and `pytest-timeout` to the test dependency group and set a global `timeout` in the pytest configuration.

**Why.** A test that only passes in file order, or hangs on a missing mock, passes on the author's machine and stalls CI for everyone else.

**Incorrect:**

```toml
[dependency-groups]
test = ["pytest"]
```

**Correct:**

```toml
[dependency-groups]
test = ["pytest", "pytest-randomly", "pytest-timeout"]

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
timeout = 60
```

## Register every marker and run pytest with --strict-markers

_medium · python, pytest_

**Rule.** Register each custom marker in `pyproject.toml` and put `--strict-markers` in `addopts`.

**Why.** A misspelled marker is only a warning, so `-m "not integration"` still runs the test you meant to leave out.

**Incorrect:**

```toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
addopts = "-ra"
```

**Correct:**

```toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
addopts = "-ra --strict-markers"
markers = ["integration: needs external services"]
```

## Run one contract suite against the database adapter and the in-memory fake

_medium · python, pytest_

**Rule.** Put the behaviour every adapter of a port must have in a class whose name does not start with
`Test`, with a `repo` fixture that raises `NotImplementedError`. Give each adapter a `Test...`
subclass that overrides `repo`: the in-memory fake in the normal run, and the database adapter
against the production engine, marked `integration`.

**Why.** Tests written separately for the fake and for the adapter drift apart, so the fake keeps accepting
what the database rejects (a duplicate key, a missing row) and the service tests built on it pass.

**Incorrect:**

```python
def test_fake_returns_none_for_unknown_id() -> None:
    assert InMemoryBookRepository().get(UUID(int=7)) is None
# the SQL adapter has its own, different tests
```

**Correct:**

```python
class BookRepositoryContract:
    @pytest.fixture
    def repo(self) -> BookRepository:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def test_unknown_id_returns_none(self, repo: BookRepository) -> None:
        assert repo.get(UUID(int=7)) is None

class TestInMemoryBookRepository(BookRepositoryContract):
    @pytest.fixture
    def repo(self) -> BookRepository:
        return InMemoryBookRepository()

@pytest.mark.integration
class TestSqlBookRepository(BookRepositoryContract):
    @pytest.fixture
    def repo(self, conn: Connection) -> BookRepository:
        return SqlBookRepository(conn)
```

## Run integration tests against the production database engine with testcontainers

_medium · python, pytest, testcontainers_

**Rule.** Start the same relational engine production uses in a session-scoped `testcontainers` fixture, give each test its own connection that is rolled back afterwards, and mark such tests `integration`.

**Why.** SQLite accepts statements and types that Postgres rejects, so the suite is green and the first production query fails; the rollback keeps the shared container from leaking data between tests.

**Incorrect:**

```python
engine = create_engine("sqlite://")   # production runs Postgres
```

**Correct:**

```python
@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def engine():
    with PostgresContainer("postgres:17") as pg:
        yield create_engine(pg.get_connection_url())

@pytest.fixture
def conn(engine):
    with engine.connect() as connection, connection.begin() as tx:
        yield connection
        tx.rollback()

@pytest.mark.integration
def test_saves_user(conn): ...
```

## Pin every counterexample Hypothesis finds as an @example

_medium · python, pytest, hypothesis_

**Rule.** For round-trips, idempotent operations and other invariants write a `@given` test. When Hypothesis finds a failing input, add it as an `@example` on that test.

**Why.** Hypothesis' local example database is not committed, so a failure it found on one machine can pass on the next run and return unnoticed, while an `@example` is replayed every time.

**Incorrect:**

```python
@given(st.dictionaries(st.text(), st.integers()))
def test_roundtrip(data):
    assert decode(encode(data)) == data   # failed on {"": 0}; fixed, not pinned
```

**Correct:**

```python
@given(st.dictionaries(st.text(), st.integers()))
@example({"": 0})   # found by Hypothesis: empty key was dropped
def test_roundtrip(data):
    assert decode(encode(data)) == data
```

## Measure branch coverage and never lower an existing fail_under

_medium · python, pytest_

**Rule.** Set `branch = true`. If the project has a `fail_under`, treat it as a regression guard: raise it when coverage rises and never lower it to make CI pass. Justify every `# pragma: no cover` in a comment.

**Why.** Line coverage counts an `if` as covered when only one branch ran, and a threshold lowered to make CI pass no longer guards anything.

**Incorrect:**

```toml
[tool.coverage.report]
fail_under = 60   # was 85, lowered to pass
```

**Correct:**

```toml
[tool.coverage.run]
branch = true

[tool.coverage.report]
fail_under = 85
```

**Exceptions.** An application that follows `testing/strategy/principles/cover-use-cases-not-lines` sets no percentage target: it keeps `branch = true` and omits `fail_under`.

## Use pytest's built-in fixtures instead of hand-rolled setup

_medium · python, pytest_

**Rule.** Use the built-in fixtures (`tmp_path`, `monkeypatch`, `capsys`, `caplog`) before writing a fixture or setup code of your own.

**Why.** Hand-rolled temp directories and patched globals have to be cleaned up by the test, and the first failure before that cleanup leaks them into the next test; the built-in fixtures undo themselves.

**Incorrect:**

```python
def test_cache_writes_file():
    directory = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    Cache(directory).put("k", "v")
    assert open(f"{directory}/k").read() == "v"
```

**Correct:**

```python
def test_cache_writes_file(tmp_path):
    Cache(tmp_path).put("k", "v")
    assert (tmp_path / "k").read_text() == "v"
```

## Keep pytest-asyncio in strict mode and mark every async test and fixture

_medium · python, pytest, pytest-asyncio_

**Rule.** Leave `pytest-asyncio` in its default `strict` mode. Mark each coroutine test with `@pytest.mark.asyncio` and each async fixture with `@pytest_asyncio.fixture`.

**Why.** In `auto` mode pytest-asyncio takes over every `async def` test, including those meant for another async plugin such as AnyIO's; in strict mode an unmarked coroutine test is not handled by pytest-asyncio, so pytest skips or fails it depending on the version.

**Incorrect:**

```python
async def test_fetch_user(client):
    assert (await client.fetch_user(1)).id == 1
```

**Correct:**

```python
@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_fetch_user(client):
    assert (await client.fetch_user(1)).id == 1
```

**Exceptions.** Use `asyncio_mode = "auto"` only when pytest-asyncio is the only async plugin in the project.

## Use plain assert and test one behaviour at a time

_medium · python, pytest_

**Rule.** Write plain `assert` statements, not `self.assertEqual`, and give each test one behaviour to check. Several `assert` lines are fine when they describe the same behaviour.

**Why.** A test that checks three behaviours gets a vague name and fails without saying which behaviour broke.

**Incorrect:**

```python
def test_discount():
    result = apply_discount(order, percent=150)
    assert result.total == Decimal("0.00")
    assert result.applied_percent == 100
    assert send_receipt.called   # a different behaviour
```

**Correct:**

```python
def test_discount_never_goes_below_zero():
    result = apply_discount(order, percent=150)
    assert result.total == Decimal("0.00")
    assert result.applied_percent == 100
```

## Choose the next test by what would hurt most if it broke

_medium · any_

**Rule.** Pick the next test by asking what in the untested part of the app would hurt most if it broke. Narrow
that to one or a few units of code, name who uses them, write the instructions you would give a manual
tester, and turn those instructions into the automated test.

**Why.** Tests chosen by walking through branches, loops and lifecycles cover code nobody would miss while the
checkout flow stays untested, so effort goes up and confidence does not.

## Give every parametrized pytest case a readable id

_low · python, pytest_

**Rule.** Give each case of `@pytest.mark.parametrize` a readable id, with `pytest.param(..., id=...)` next to its data or an `ids=` list.

**Why.** Anonymous ids such as `test_add[1-2-3]` do not say which case failed or what it was meant to cover.

**Incorrect:**

```python
@pytest.mark.parametrize(("a", "b", "expected"), [(1, 2, 3), (-1, 1, 0)])
def test_add(a: int, b: int, expected: int) -> None:
    assert add(a, b) == expected
```

**Correct:**

```python
@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    ("a", "b", "expected"),
    [pytest.param(1, 2, 3, id="positives"), pytest.param(-1, 1, 0, id="cancel-out")],
)
def test_add(a: int, b: int, expected: int) -> None:
    assert add(a, b) == expected
```
